The global Internet of Things (IoT) network has experienced unprecedented expansion, reaching 75.44 billion connected devices worldwide. Due to this rapid growth, the IoT ecosystem has become larger but also more vulnerable to various threats in cyberspace. As a result, this situation has accelerated the development of more complex cyberattacks, especially Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks, which can damage systems by overwhelming network traffic. This attack exploits the inherent vulnerabilities of IoT networks with limited resources, leading to significant service interruptions, monetary losses, and potentially the failure of vital infrastructures. As a result, this survey presents a new taxonomy of attack types, a thorough assessment of conventional and AI-driven detection techniques, and a comparison of advanced countermeasures. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive and systematic overview of DDoS attack detection, prevention, and mitigation approaches for the IoT. A major contribution of this work is the inclusion of blockchain-based security frameworks, federated learning, deep learning, machine learning, and quantum computing paradigms in its discussion for reducing DDoS attacks on the IoT. Furthermore, real-world case studies highlight the severe impact of such attacks on mission-critical domains, including smart cities, healthcare, and industrial control systems (ICSs). This survey provides a basis for cybersecurity researchers, security experts, and hobbyists, grounded in the understanding gained from previous research.
topics: Internet Traffic Analysis and Secure E-voting

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming education by enabling personalized learning pathways, automating tasks, and creating interactive technologies that expand access. Recent reports show that 87% of schools worldwide have adopted AI tools in some form, and the AI-in-education market is projected to grow from $5.88 billion in 2024 to $32.3 billion by 2030 ( Grand View Research, 2025 ; SQ Magazine, 2025 ). This review highlights how AI enhances individualized learning, improves student engagement, and streamlines administration. Simultaneously, challenges such as privacy risks, algorithmic bias, and the digital divide remain. Global frameworks from UNESCO emphasize that without strong ethical policies, AI can deepen inequalities rather than reduce them. This paper adopted a structural literature review approach that synthesized global reports, peer-reviewed studies, and policy documents to map out current trends. The paper concludes that AI&s;s potential in education can be realized only through responsible adoption, professional development for educators, and inclusive infrastructure investments. This paper integrates global adoption statistics with ethical and equity perspectives, highlighting the research gap in empirical classroom-based studies. These implications suggest that policymakers and educators must balance innovation with safeguards to ensure equitable outcomes.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven personalization has increasingly transformed digital marketing by enabling firms to deliver individualized recommendations, content, and offers based on consumer data and behavioral patterns. However, the growing use of personalization also raises important questions regarding consumer trust, engagement, and purchase behavior. This study aims to conduct a systematic literature review (SLR) of research on AI-driven personalization in digital marketing to examine its implications for consumer trust, engagement, and purchase behavior. Using Scopus as the primary database, the search process identified 2,906 records and, through successive filtering and screening procedures, resulted in 51 eligible studies. Bibliometric analysis using VOSviewer and thematic synthesis were employed to identify publication trends, intellectual structures, and key research themes. The findings indicate a shift from technology-oriented research toward consumer-centered perspectives, with increasing attention to consumer experience, trust, engagement, privacy, transparency, purchase intention, and purchase behavior. The review further demonstrates that the effectiveness of AI-driven personalization is context-dependent and influenced by consumer perceptions and data-related concerns. These findings provide an integrated basis for understanding the evolving role of AI personalization in contemporary digital marketing

Abstract Public-sector building retrofits in the United Kingdom require decisions that balance whole-life cost, carbon reduction, service continuity and auditability under limited data and constrained capital budgets. This paper develops a decision-ready whole-life costing (WLC) workflow that integrates environmental, social and governance (ESG) priorities with uncertainty-aware artificial intelligence (AI) for public-building retrofit appraisal. The workflow combines national non-domestic Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) and Display Energy Certificate (DEC) data, Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme (PSDS) delivery evidence and stakeholder inputs to construct a scenario library of public-building archetypes, retrofit actions and appraisal constraints. Stakeholder priorities from interviews, a questionnaire and a co-design workshop are translated into transparent weights using fuzzy analytic hierarchy process (F-AHP). These weights parameterise a reinforcement learning (RL) planner, while a Bayesian convolutional neural network–long short-term memory (BCNN–LSTM) surrogate provides uncertainty-bounded energy, carbon and cost trajectories for repeated policy evaluation. Results show that the workflow supports auditable retrofit sequencing across archetype and budget conditions and improves composite ESG performance relative to conventional WLC-only, £/tCO 2 e and static multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) baselines. For 1000 matched archetype–budget cases, the trained deep Q-network (DQN) decision-search stage achieves a 30.03-fold speedup over traditional scalar feasible-sequence enumeration. The contribution is an integrated and explainable WLC–ESG–AI workflow for early-stage public retrofit decision support. The current validation remains based on public datasets and scenario-level evidence so future work should extend the framework using project-specific metered data, digital twins and live portfolio deployment.

Artificial intelligence has structurally transformed financial phishing, collapsing the cost of personalised attacks; India recorded 135,173 financial phishing attacks in H1 2024, a 175% rise over 2023. This chapter examines the convergence of AI-enabled phishing, student data vulnerability, and digital literacy deficits in India's skill-based educational institutions (ITIs, polytechnics, skill universities), a population absent from existing cybersecurity literature despite holding data regulated under the DPDP Act, 2023. Drawing on Routine Activity Theory, Protection Motivation Theory, the Digital Literacy Continuum, and Institutional Theory, it develops the Protection Gap construct and a Four-Layer Institutional Defence Model. A primary survey (N = 96, seven states) finds 66.7% encountered suspected phishing, mostly via WhatsApp; only 25.0% identified a genuine message; 59.4% were unaware of the DPDP Act; and 43.8% reported no explicit consent for Aadhaar/bank data. The chapter closes with recommendations for MeitY, AICTE, NSDC, and the Data Protection Board of India.

Abstract Wearable sensing and artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly being used to quantify athlete movement, physiological response, training load, and recovery in field and laboratory settings. However, the practical value of these systems depends not only on the predictive capability of an algorithm but also on sensor validity, signal quality, hardware constraints, real-time processing, and the transferability of models across athletes and sports. This review examines the technical pipeline linking wearable electronic sensors to athlete-monitoring decisions, with particular attention to inertial measurement units, global navigation satellite systems, photoplethysmography, electrocardiography, electromyography, pressure sensing, and multimodal systems. It synthesizes evidence on signal conditioning, segmentation, feature engineering, classical machine learning, deep learning, sensor fusion, edge inference, and embedded implementation. Existing reviews indicate that wearable devices can support useful monitoring, but accuracy varies by metric, device, movement pattern, and validation setting; performance under controlled conditions should not be assumed to generalize to competition. Key challenges include motion artifacts, inconsistent protocols, small and imbalanced datasets, leakage between training and test sets, limited external validation, battery and communication constraints, privacy, and unclear decision thresholds. The review proposes a layered reference architecture and a validation framework that links engineering performance to sport-specific usefulness. Future research should prioritize synchronized multimodal datasets, athlete-independent testing, interpretable and uncertainty-aware models, energy-efficient edge AI, secure data governance, and transparent reporting. The article’s contribution is an engineering-oriented synthesis that connects sensor physics and embedded constraints with the needs of physical education and sports science. The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has accelerated the development of deepfake technology, enabling the creation of highly realistic fabricated audio, video, and visual content that closely resembles authentic media. A mixed-method approach was employed, combining an online survey of 47 Namibian internet users and a total of 12 key informants were interviewed. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics, while qualitative data were subjected to thematic analysis. The findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge on deepfake technologies by providing empirical evidence from Namibia and offering practical recommendations for enhancing digital literacy, strengthening regulatory frameworks, and improving institutional preparedness.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Radiological examinations increasingly leverage artificial intelligence to enhance diagnostic performance by compensating for expertise shortages, particularly in specialized interpretation. Despite academic AI models achieving compelling accuracy, adoption remains low. An objective, evidence-based examination of AI-guided clinical image interpretation seeks to expose the underlying reasons. The primary challenge lies not in accuracy but in fully automated analysis, especially for multimodal and multidimensional datasets. Introduction of uncertainty measures, image explainability, and real-world data reduce recognition to a decisive-supporting role—helping radiologists to detect previously unnoticed abnormalities—or even to precautionary analysis. Patients requesting precision medicine and therapy planning—and those at high risk of neglected pathology—stand to gain the greatest benefit. Relevant AI architecture considers imaging cues suitable for precision medicine or requiring additional methods to obtain interpretable images. Successful performance testing against an external, hidden reference dataset promotes vital user trust. Machine learning achieves best results where all potentially pathological abnormalities are identified and their presence virtually guaranteed, as in multi-class recognition. Data scarcity, however, impedes clinically relevant solutions. Explainability, essential for medical applications and clinical acceptance, extends simply beyond clinical decision support to provide saliency maps and, better still, clinically meaningful image regions or qualities. Attention maps may even bring a form of rule-based reasoning within reach. Clinical integration that reproduces the technical conditions under which model diagnostic measures are calculated raises the challenge of uncertainty quantification—a necessary condition for clinical decision support. Convolutional neural networks trained for photo-quality classification, par excellence supervised image quality assessment, provide the basic cues for uncertainty quantification. Imaging acquisition, modality, and systems are also defined in terms of current PACS/EPIC systems. PE, pre-symptomatic examination or precautionary examination, is defined as a patient-user group prepared to cover the cost of an examination with lower diagnostic accuracy and a high level of uncertainty.

documents.abstract: This repository accompanies the manuscript "When AI Speaks for Heritage: Algorithmic Visibility, Channel-Size Confounds, and the Authenticity Backlash in AI-Mediated Intangible Cultural Heritage on YouTube", submitted to Telematics and Informatics Reports (Special Issue: Cultural Heritage and AI for Strategic Communication, Digital Innovation, and Global Engagement). **Data:** per-video metadata and final labels (videos_final_labels.csv), channel metadata, raw and labelled comment corpora, per-coder LLM labels, and the 31-video adjudication + 300-video human-validation records. **Prompts:** verbatim system/user prompts for all five LLM coders and the comment classifier. **Code:** the end-to-end pipeline from platform pull through labelling to analysis and validation; analysis.py reproduces every number in the manuscript. All data are publicly available YouTube metadata and public comments (no private data; no API keys committed; credentials read from environment variables). Licence: CC-0 (data), CC-BY-4.0 (code). Public from submission, no embargo.

The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) based robo-advisor has become a disruptive game-changer in the field of investment advisory service, altering the manner in which portfolios are managed as well as how individuals are making investing choices. These platforms provide cost-efficient, personalized and scalable financial recommendations using Big data analytics, machine learning, and algorithmic automation. The paper is a systematic literature review carried out with the help of PRISMA to draw generalizations on the available literature on the topic of AI-powered robo-advisors, the basics behind their technology, the impact on investor behavior, the performance of their portfolios, and the ethical and regulatory issues related to this field. Based on the searches of peer-reviewed published literature published in 2016-2025, the review determines the main themes in the context of decision accuracy, reduction of behavioral bias, risk optimization, and democratization of financial advice. The results reveal that the efficiency and objectiveness of investment management is considerably increased by robo-advisors, but the issues of data privacy, algorithmic transparency, and regulation are raised. The paper concludes that hybrid advisory models that integrate AI with the human judgment skills are the most sustainable future of the investment advisory services. New issues of data privacy, algorithmic transparency, ethical fairness, and regulatory compliance are critically looked into as well as those benefits such as automation, objectivity, accessibility and democratization of financial advice are identified. It argues in the study that hybrid models of advising that integrate AI capabilities with human decision-making will probably Explain the future of the investment guidance services utilising real case studies and research that is currently available.

ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is creating new possibilities for connecting research‐led teaching with authentic industry projects, yet its educational value depends on how educators organize inquiry rather than on technological use alone. This study examined the relationships among AI‐supported research‐led teaching (AIRLT), educator questioning (EQ), educator feedback (EF), student inquiry engagement (SIE), and authentic project learning outcomes (APLO) within Syntegrative Project‐Based Learning. A quantitative cross‐sectional survey was conducted with 898 undergraduate students from 12 universities in Vietnam who had participated in authentic industry or organizational projects involving AI‐supported inquiry and educator guidance. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS‐SEM) showed that AIRLT was positively associated with EQ ( β = 0.642) and EF ( β = 0.611). Both EQ ( β = 0.463) and EF ( β = 0.349) were positively associated with SIE, which, in turn, showed a strong positive association with APLO ( β = 0.689). All six specific indirect effects were significant, indicating statistically significant indirect associations among AI‐supported teaching, educator guidance, student inquiry, and perceived authentic learning outcomes. The findings contribute an educator‐mediated perspective to Syntegrative Education by showing that AI is most educationally meaningful when embedded in purposeful questioning, feedback, and sustained student inquiry. The study highlights the importance of designing AI‐supported industry projects around evidence evaluation, iterative feedback, reflection, and active investigation of authentic problems rather than treating AI use as an educational objective in itself.

ABSTRACT Firms increasingly incorporate generative and non‐generative artificial intelligence (AI) into product design, formulation, and production, and they face a disclosure question: how should they describe the role of AI to consumers? Across six studies, including analysis of 1800 marketplace listings and five pre‐registered experiments (total experimental N = 2760), we introduce and test a 2‐by‐2 framework of algorithmic provenance defined by the AI's role (agentic vs. assistive) and its visibility in the final product (visible vs. invisible). Identical products are evaluated differently depending on where they fall in this taxonomy. Agentic AI involvement (AI as designer) reduces consumer product attitudes, perceived quality, purchase intentions, and willingness to pay relative to assistive AI involvement (AI as a tool for a human designer). The effect is amplified when AI involvement is visible in the final product. The downstream responses are partially mediated by a new construct, perceived authenticity of creative intention, which captures consumers' inference about whether a human creator pursued a genuine creative vision. The effect is larger for expressive than for functional product domains and larger among consumers primed to hold an independent self‐construal. A scalable managerial intervention, creative‐intent framing, narrows the agentic penalty by approximately half, again through the authenticity mechanism. The findings identify a substantively important new construct for AI disclosure research, refine theories of algorithmic aversion, and offer marketers an actionable disclosure design principle.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Small variations in prompt characteristics can meaningfully alter the semantics, tone, and contextual assumptions of large language model outputs. Such characteristics can involve group variables such as demographics or other sensitive latent attributes. Sensitivity to such input variables is undesirable when demographic information is causally irrelevant to the task, but might still be relevant for generation of semantically coherent responses. This makes the task of enforcing counterfactual invariance while preserving model utility difficult. To study this problem, we first show that standard model alignment recipes (such as reinforcement learning) increase differences in response quality across demographics, while improving overall response quality, ultimately amplifying what is known as counterfactual bias. To address this, we develop a policy gradient technique involving a group-level reward function that operates on matched pairs of counterfactual prompts. For completeness, we build a dataset of controlled counterfactual prompt pairs and design an evaluation that separately measures cases where demographic information is causally relevant to the answer. Finally, we validate our findings on several fairness benchmarks. We demonstrate that our methods reduce counterfactual differences while preserving overall response quality and that the models continue to adapt appropriately when such sensitive information is relevant.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: As LLM-based agents are deployed with increasing autonomy in real-world environments, a critical failure mode emerges: agentic misalignment, where agents choose harmful actions over failure. However, existing safety benchmarks primarily evaluate whether agents comply with explicitly harmful instructions, leaving the conditions that cause agents to choose harmful actions poorly understood. To address this limitation, we propose AM-Bench, a unified taxonomy and 35 scenario evaluation benchmark spanning seven industries for agentic misalignment grounded in the fraud triangle, a well-established criminological framework explaining goal-directed misconduct. We adapt this framework to agentic environments and construct our evaluation suite and detection systems along three dimensions: perceived threat, perceived opportunity, and reasoning. We operationalize each dimension into structured subcategories rooted in prior theory: five threat categories derived from the instrumental convergence thesis, seven opportunity categories drawn from the Emergent Strategic Reasoning Risks (ESRR) taxonomy, and a novel four-question binary reasoning framework synthesized from prior literature. Our evaluation of 10 frontier models reveals a 62-percentage-point gap in misalignment across scenarios, with Gemini 3 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro exhibiting the highest levels of agentic misalignment while Claude Sonnet 4.6 displays near-zero rates across all conditions. Our reasoning framework further reveals that models may exhibit harmful behaviours without explicit situational awareness or explanation, complicating both mitigation and detection. AM-Bench scenarios and code are available at https://github.com/AI4Collaboration/Agentic-Misalignment-Bench
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Network-on-Chip (NoC) architectures have become a fundamental communication backbone for many-core processors, artificial intelligence accelerators, edge-computing platforms, and high-performance embedded systems. However, achieving efficient packet routing in large-scale NoCs remains challenging due to dynamic traffic variations, congestion propagation, limited global network visibility, and stringent hardware constraints. Conventional deterministic and heuristic routing algorithms suffer from reduced adaptability under non-uniform traffic conditions, whereas existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based routers primarily rely on local state representations and finite-state-machine (FSM) controllers, limiting their scalability, topology awareness, and hardware deployability. To address these limitations, this work proposes an Adaptive Congestion-Aware Graph Neural Routing Framework with Hybrid Microcoded Event-Driven Control for Network-on-Chip Systems. The proposed framework integrates three complementary components: (i) an Adaptive Congestion-Aware Graph Neural Network (ACA-GNN) encoder that generates compact topology-aware embeddings by capturing local and multi-hop congestion dependencies through congestion-aware message propagation, (ii) a quantized Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) agent that performs low-latency adaptive routing decisions using compact graph embeddings, and (iii) a Hybrid Microcoded Event-Driven Controller (H-µEDC) that replaces conventional FSM-based control with programmable event-triggered micro-routines to ensure deterministic routing execution. The proposed architecture is implemented on a Xilinx Zynq-7000 FPGA and evaluated using BookSim2 cycle-accurate simulation, Orion 3.0 power modeling, synthetic traffic patterns, and PARSEC/Rodinia benchmark workloads. Experimental results demonstrate up to 48% lower packet latency, and 31% lower energy per flit compared with state-of-the-art heuristic and machine-learning-based routing approaches. Hardware implementation further requires only 1.2% LUTs, 1.4% flip-flops, three DSP blocks, one BRAM, and 0.556 W power consumption while maintaining deterministic single-cycle routing decisions using cached ACA-GNN embeddings. These results demonstrate that the proposed ACA-GNN-HµEDC framework effectively combines topology-aware routing intelligence, congestion adaptivity, hardware efficiency, and scalability, making it a practical solution for next-generation many-core Network-on-Chip systems.

Predicting student performance has become a vital objective in educational data mining, however existing models remain limited by limited feature sets, opaque decision processes, and the absence of real-time, context-aware interpretative intelligence. This study presents a novel hybrid Artificial Intelligence (AI) architecture that integrates cognitive, emotional, and general intelligence indicators with formative assessment/class performance data to construct a multidimensional demonstration of student performance. The system utilizes a mathematically formalized feature-weighting mechanism that allows domain experts to regulate the influence of key predictors prior to training, enabling a tunable and educator-configurable modeling process. Interaction between cognitive, emotional, and behavioral properties are explicitly engineered to capture complex effects often overlooked in prior research. An ensemble predictive model combining Random Forests, Gradient Boosting, and Linear Regression is used to predict student grades, with uncertainty measured through variance-based confidence intervals. The integrated system exhibited strong predictive capability, attaining high accuracy (R 2 = 0.9014, 95% CI [0.8882, 0.9121], 10,000 bootstrap resamples) with low prediction error, confirming the stability and reliability of the ensemble model. Understanding why a model produces a particular prediction is often as important as the prediction itself. To address the interpretability gap, the system incorporates SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based global and local explanations, a counterfactual simulation engine that estimates the marginal impact of improving specific attributes, and a local generative AI layer deployed via Ollama that creates these outputs into structured, real-time narrative feedback. Running the Large Language Model (LLM) locally ensures privacy-preserving, institution-compliant interpretability while permitting interactive, student specific explanations. This integration of predictive modeling, explainability, simulation, and local generative reasoning creates a unified decision-support framework that exceeds traditional black-box approaches. Experimental assessment shows that the model not only achieves viable predictive accuracy but also provides actionable insights into feature influence, model stability, and potential intervention pathways.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Wearable human–machine interfaces (HMIs) are at the forefront of next‐generation intelligent systems, demanding interfaces that are not only accurate and responsive, but also ergonomic, stretchable, and seamlessly integrated into daily life. In this work, we present a novel HMI system enabled by a glove and garment, based on fully textile, matrix‐free capacitive strain sensors (CSSs). Our sensor is fabricated via a single‐step, sewing‐machine‐compatible double‐twisted knitting process of silver‐coated knitted textile electrodes and a nylon/elastane textile dielectric, eliminating the need for post‐processing, polymer encapsulation, or rigid substrates. The resulting all‐fabric CSS demonstrates a high gauge factor of 2.03 over a broad strain range (0–72%), with excellent linearity (R 2 = 0.982), hysteresis (7.80%), and minimal signal creep. The textile‐based architecture preserves garment‐level wearability, with the nylon/elastane dielectric exhibiting a porosity of ∼66%, while the silver‐coated textile electrode (∼77% porosity) maintains a low and stable resistance (∼4.4 Ω) under 0–60% strain. Integrated into a wearable glove, the proposed system enables detection of 10 distinct hand gestures with recognition accuracy of 90.5%. This work marks a significant advancement toward fully textile‐integrated, breathable, comfortable, stretchable, and high‐performance HMI solutions, with broad implications for virtual environments, assistive technologies, and next‐generation wearable robotics.
topics: Advanced Sensor and Energy Harvesting Materials

documents.abstract: Glacial Isostatic Adjustment (GIA) models solve the gravitationally self-consistent sea-level equation for the response of the solid Earth and the oceans to changing ice loads. As these models are increasingly embedded in coupled ice-sheet simulations, glacial-cycle calculations, and large ensembles, standard pseudo-spectral 1-D solvers face a steep computational barrier: they evaluate the viscoelastic response by explicitly re-summing every past load increment, scaling quadratically with time steps as $O(N^2)$. Here we show that this computational penalty is an artifact of algorithmic formulation rather than Earth physics. By exploiting the exponential form of the viscoelastic relaxation kernel, we reformulate the viscous response as an exact recursive update of a finite set of modal states, without re-summing the load history. This exact reformulation alone reduces the cost of a run to $O(N)$, yielding a 20.6-fold speed-up relative to a standard full-history 1-D GIA solver for a case study involving a 550-step Antarctic future sea-level projection. Implemented in our open-source solver SLEvolve v1.0, this formulation---combined with fewer, table-free and multithreaded spherical-harmonic transforms, improved file handling, and physics-inspired iteration starts---achieves an end-to-end speed-up of over three orders of magnitude (up to 4,000-fold) against the same 1-D GIA solver, reducing day-long simulations to under thirty seconds on a workstation. Beyond this solid-Earth application, SLEvolve illustrates how human-derived analytical reformulations can be combined with benchmark-harnessed AI-assisted engineering to modernize scientific software. In particular, Numerical regression tests and performance profiling guided the AI agents' implementation choices and helped reject ineffective optimizations.

documents.abstract: The new materials industry is a strategic pillar industry underpinning China's pursuit of technological self-reliance and self-strengthening. It plays a vital role in the development of advanced manufacturing, the achievement of the "dual carbon" goals, and the security of industrial and supply chains. The deep integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) with materials Research and Development (R&D) is continuously reshaping the innovation and production models of the industry. Existing literature has extensively examined new materials technologies and AI-driven innovation, but relatively little research has systematically analyzed the competitive landscape of the industry from the perspective of industrial economics. Clarifying the characteristics of industry competition can provide practical insights for domestic industrial policymaking and overseas industrial deployment under the framework of the Belt and Road Initiative. Using Porter's Five Forces model as the analytical framework, this study examines the competitive characteristics of China's new materials industry by drawing on publicly available industry reports, existing literature, and online interviews with industry practitioners, given the constraints on obtaining first-hand corporate research samples. The findings indicate that the industry as a whole has high entry barriers, while supplier bargaining power varies significantly across different segments. Buyers and substitutes exert moderate competitive pressure, and the intensity of intra-industry competition differs substantially between low-end and high-end segments. Based on these findings, corresponding industrial policy recommendations are proposed, followed by a discussion of the limitations of this study and directions for future research.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) perform well on audio-visual question answering, but correct answers do not necessarily imply that their stated reasoning is grounded in relevant perceptual evidence. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate final-answer accuracy, offering limited insight into whether model-generated rationales correctly identify visual regions, temporal intervals, and audio events supporting predictions. We introduce ANCHOR, a benchmark and evaluation framework for measuring grounded-rationale alignment in multimodal reasoning, comprising 2,319 videos and 8,272 question-answer pairs with structured reasoning traces, temporal evidence, spatial bounding boxes, and salient audio cues, including a human-refined test set of 224 videos and 975 question-answer pairs. We separately measure answer correctness, hallucination, logical divergence, and conciseness, with direct spatial and temporal grounding measurements on a focused subset. Across the full benchmark, twelve contemporary MLLMs show a substantial alignment gap: models with comparable answer performance can differ markedly in whether their explanations are supported by annotated evidence. On a matched subset of 100 videos and 446 question-answer pairs, rankings remain highly stable across human-refined, Gemini-generated, and GPT-generated references (mean Pearson r=0.99), providing evidence against model-reference circularity within this subset. Grounding-cue ablations of three MLLMs on the full human-refined test set reveal a consistent modality hierarchy: removing video reduces accuracy by 38.4-41.8 points, while removing bounding boxes (3.2-7.7 points) and audio (4.2-5.6 points) causes smaller, complementary, model-dependent drops. These findings show answer-only evaluation obscures important grounding failures and position ANCHOR as a testbed for evaluating accurate and evidence-aligned audio-visual reasoning.

Every study of why LLM agents fail begins by labelling traces by hand, and every such study builds its own throwaway tool. Observability platforms record agent traces but offer no structured labelling; annotation tools label text but have no notion of a step, a delegation or a tool call, leaving it unclear what the smallest unit of execution to label should be. Annotrace reads six trace formats, including OpenTelemetry GenAI, LangSmith and Langfuse, and turns each run into an ordered, nested list of steps. The annotator writes their own labelling codebook; a frontier model proposes a starting set from a sample of their own traces, answers first, and is asked exactly the questions the human is asked, making annotation a joint human-AI process. Annotrace measures agreement between any two annotators, human or AI. On a multi-agent question-answering corpus it reproduces a previous manual effort's 235 annotation units exactly, and two models labelling the same traces agree 91% of the time at $κ= 0.82$.

Cerebral palsy (CP) is a neurological disorder characterized by impaired movement, balance difficulties, abnormal muscle tone, and motor dysfunction resulting from brain damage during early developmental stages of birth. These impairments significantly influence a child’s ability to perform daily activities and lead an independent life. Therefore, providing appropriate assistive mobility devices is essential to enhance mobility, safety, and overall quality of life for children with CP. Walking aids are commonly used rehabilitation devices designed to support movement and promote independence. Many existing walking aids are not designed using anthropometric data representative of the geographical population for which they are intended, which may reduce their ergonomic suitability. This study addresses this limitation by developing a local anthropometric database for Jordanian children with CP aged 1–5 years. Anthropometric measurements were collected and analyzed to support ergonomic design requirements. Based on these measurements, dimensional requirements were established and translated into a conceptual computer-aided design (CAD) of an adjustable walking aid. The proposed conceptual design incorporates appropriate dimensional specifications derived from the collected anthropometric data to ensure comfort, stability, and safety. Jansen mechanism of motion is applied to the new design to promote children mobility. The proposed walking aid is intended to accommodate children with CP within the 1–5-year age group, facilitating improved mobility and supporting their participation in daily activities and rehabilitation programs.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: AI services are prone to moral hazard, as model providers can silently route requests to cheaper, lower-quality models, and the inherent stochasticity of model outputs makes this degradation hard to detect. Contract theory addresses moral hazard by designing payment rules that reward high-quality outputs and prevent strategic overcharging. However, existing frameworks assume interactions of fixed duration, whereas AI services are typically consumed through subscriptions and pay-as-you-go APIs that users can terminate at any time based on observed performance. We show that this flexibility can break standard contracts, opening them up to abuse by either the providers or users. To address this, we extend contract theory to account for unknown exit rules. We formalize the problem as a Principal-Agent game, and show that budget-optimal contracts in this setting are proportional to anytime-valid hypothesis tests based on likelihood-ratio e-values. We give an efficient algorithm for computing anytime contracts and show how betting e-processes can be used to approximate them when the models are unknown. Finally, we evaluate our findings on synthetic data and data from deployed LLMs.

The Human Factors Analysis and Classification System (HFACS) is increasingly used and modified in maritime accident research. This study is a systematic review of the use of HFACS in maritime research. Bibliometric patterns in Web of Science (WoS) and Scopus are investigated. The study used a combination of systematic review, content analysis and bibliometric mapping according to the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The final datasets of WoS and Scopus included 60 studies each, of which 55 were common to both databases, resulting in a total of 65 unique eligible studies. The results show a recent growth in maritime HFACS research, mainly concentrated in China and Türkiye. HFACS is still in widespread use, but a number of maritime-specific adaptations have been proposed and HFACS has been combined with probabilistic, system-oriented and data-driven methods. Analyzing the ten most-cited and ten database-specific studies identified causal factors at different HFACS levels and mitigation measures addressing operational and organizational issues. The citation-network structures of WoS and Scopus were different, but the frequently occurring keywords and highly cited publications and authors were similar. In general, the results show that maritime HFACS research has progressed beyond accident classification by the use of adapted frameworks and complementary analytical methods.

Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming professional services through automation, information processing, analytics and decision support. Legal and accounting professions, which rely on expertise, judgment, confidentiality and compliance, are increasingly exposed to AI technologies, though adoption and perceived impacts may differ between the two fields. This study examines and compares AI adoption and professional transformation among legal and accounting professionals in Mumbai. It focuses on AI awareness, adoption, perceived benefits, professional transformation, ethical concerns, skills, employment implications and future adoption intentions. A quantitative research design using a structured questionnaire will be adopted, with data analysed through descriptive, reliability, correlation and comparative statistical techniques. The study aims to identify similarities, differences and factors influencing AI adoption, providing insights for effective AI training, governance and responsible adoption. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, AI Adoption, Legal Professionals, Accounting Professionals, Professional Transformation, Technology Adoption, Mumbai

The integration of artificial intelligence and search technology is transforming traditional online shopping models, particularly cross-border e-commerce (CBEC), which involves complex customer multi-attribute decision-making with numerous considerations. This study systematically examines the influence of artificial intelligence on the high-quality advancement of CBEC and its underlying mechanisms using panel data from 30 Chinese provinces covering the period 2013–2023. The study found a significant positive correlation between artificial intelligence and cross-border e-commerce. This conclusion remains valid after a series of robustness tests (including removing the interference of pandemic-related data, substituting core explanatory variables, substituting the dependent variable, and lagging explanatory variables by one period). Mechanism analysis indicates that the positive impact of AI on the high-quality development of cross-border e-commerce is realized through improvements in logistics capabilities and the unlocking of consumer potential, with mediation effects accounting for 40.27% and 17.02%, respectively. Threshold model results show that the positive impact of AI on the high-quality development of cross-border e-commerce exhibits a single threshold effect based on the level of human capital; once human capital exceeds the threshold value, the coefficient further increases. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that AI has the most significant empowering effect on the development of cross-border e-commerce in the eastern regions; however, its impact on the central and western regions is relatively minor. It is worth noting that AI exerts its empowering effect more effectively in regions with high e-commerce procurement activity, whereas the relationship is not significant in regions with low activity.

documents.abstract: Although international scholarship on AI in education had expanded rapidly, empirical evidence concerning its relationship with the reading and writing skills of secondary-school students in Pakistan had remained limited. The present study examined the relationship between AI use and the reading and writing performance of male students enrolled in public secondary schools in District Sialkot, Punjab. A quantitative, cross-sectional, correlational research design was adopted. The population comprised male students enrolled in Grades 9 and 10 in government secondary schools, from whom a multistage stratified random sample of 270 students was selected. Data were collected through an AI Use in Learning Questionnaire, a researcher-developed reading comprehension test, and an analytical writing performance test. The study differentiated between productive and substitutive forms of AI use. Productive use involved explanation seeking, guided practice, idea generation, verification, formative feedback, and reflective revision, whereas substitutive use involved outsourcing comprehension and composition, copying AI-generated responses, and accepting machine-generated content without critical evaluation. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, analysis of variance, and hierarchical multiple regression were employed to examine the relationships among the variables. The study provided a contextually grounded framework for understanding AI-supported literacy, assessment integrity, digital inequality, teacher mediation, and responsible technology integration in Pakistani secondary education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence ("AI") is increasingly becoming embedded in activities that were traditionally governed by direct human judgment. Automated systems now assist in recruitment, credit assessment, healthcare, education, content generation, surveillance and public administration. The legal significance of this development lies not merely in the sophistication of the technology but in the possibility that consequential decisions may be produced through systems whose operation is difficult for affected individuals to understand or challenge. This creates questions concerning privacy, equality, discrimination, intellectual property, liability, procedural fairness and the allocation of responsibility among developers, deployers and users. India presently addresses these concerns through a combination of constitutional principles, information-technology legislation, data-protection law, sectoral regulation and policy initiatives rather than through a comprehensive AI statute. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, together with the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, has strengthened India's data-governance architecture, but data protection alone cannot resolve the wider accountability problems created by AI. This article examines the principal legal challenges associated with AI and compares India's developing approach with the European Union's risk-based Artificial Intelligence Act and the United States' standards-oriented approach. It argues that India's future AI governance should preserve a legally traceable chain of responsibility whenever decision-making is delegated to automated systems. Such a framework should combine risk classification, meaningful human oversight, transparency, privacy safeguards, anti-discrimination measures, lifecycle accountability and effective remedies. Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming organizational processes, occupational roles, skill requirements and employee expectations. Although AI has the potential to improve productivity and create new employment opportunities, its increasing use may also generate employee concerns regarding job replacement, skill obsolescence, career continuity and employment security. These concerns are particularly relevant in knowledge-intensive and technology-enabled sectors such as real estate, where artificial intelligence, data analytics, automation, digital platforms and intelligent decision-support systems are increasingly influencing organizational activities. The present study develops and proposes an empirical model examining the relationship between Artificial Intelligence Anxiety (AIA) and Employee Engagement (EE) among employees in the Indian real estate sector. Specifically, the study investigates Perceived Job Insecurity (PJI) as a mediating mechanism and Perceived Organizational Support (POS) as a moderating resource. The theoretical foundation integrates Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) theory, Conservation of Resources (COR) theory and Organizational Support Theory. The proposed model suggests that AI anxiety increases perceived job insecurity, which subsequently reduces employee engagement. Perceived organizational support is expected to weaken the positive relationship between AI anxiety and perceived job insecurity and consequently buffer the negative indirect effect of AI anxiety on employee engagement. Data will be collected using established measurement instruments for AI anxiety, job insecurity, perceived organizational support and employee engagement. Structural Equation Modelling (SEM), preferably using SmartPLS, will be employed to assess the measurement and structural models, including mediation, moderation and moderated mediation. The proposed study contributes to the emerging literature on the human consequences of AI by moving beyond technology adoption and productivity perspectives and examining the psychological pathway through which AI- related concerns influence employee engagement.

With delayed access to specialist expertise and subjective interpretation by clinicians and workload limiting the ability to access parts of the pathway, early disease detection is one of the most impactful levers that can be used to improve patient outcomes and reduce the cost of care.Medical image analysis, electronic health records (EHR), genomic data analysis, and analysis of physiological signals are all examples of medical data that can be transformed by artificial intelligence (AI) and especially machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), as there is no way they could be analyzed at the same scale and speed as would be possible by a human being.In this paper we bring together existing evidence of the use of AI in early detection in oncology, cardiology, neurology, dermatology, ophthalmology and critical care.It discusses the mathematical approaches used for their analysis such as the use of convolutional neural networks for image analysis and recurrent networks for time-series analysis of physiological data, and compares their reported diagnostic performance with that of conventional clinical analyses.The paper also examines real-world challenges to adoption, such as standardization of data, algorithmic bias, regulatory approval processes and clinician acceptance, and proposes some solutions.The results suggest that AI systems perform as well as or better than humans in precisely defined detection tasks but will not automatically translate this to better population health outcomes without attention to data quality, the need to integrate AI systems into workflows, and the need to ensure that everyone has access to them.The paper ends with policy, research and system recommendations for maximizing early detection programmatic value while responsibly scaling these initiatives.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Otolaryngology is among the medical specialties most suitable for the application of artificial intelligence (AI), largely due to the wide variety of data generated in daily practice. Otoscopic and endoscopic images, voice recordings, audiological tests, vestibular assessments, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and digital pathology slides provide rich sources of information that can be analyzed using AI-based methods. As a result, AI has emerged as a valuable tool for tasks such as image classification, segmentation, risk prediction, outcome estimation, and optimization of clinical workflows. Despite growing scientific interest, however, many AI studies in otolaryngology remain at the developmental stage and have not yet undergone sufficient clinical validation for routine use. Currently, the most practical applications of AI involve well-defined and repetitive clinical tasks. These include supporting newborn hearing screening programs, predicting cochlear implant outcomes, interpreting otoscopic and nasal endoscopic images, assisting vestibular assessments, analyzing voice recordings for laryngeal disorders, and improving risk stratification in head and neck oncology. In contrast, complex clinical decisions that require comprehensive patient evaluation continue to depend on physician expertise, with AI functioning primarily as a supportive technology rather than an independent decision-maker. The future role of AI in otolaryngology is therefore not to replace clinicians but to enhance decision-making by improving efficiency, consistency, and data utilization. Successful implementation will require not only high diagnostic accuracy but also careful attention to validation, data quality, patient privacy, regulatory oversight, and clinical accountability. Consequently, the major challenge ahead is not the development of new algorithms, but their safe and responsible integration into clinical practice.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Retinal degenerative diseases, including age-related macular degeneration (AMD), retinitis pigmentosa (RP), and Stargardt disease, represent leading causes of irreversible vision loss worldwide, collectively affecting hundreds of millions of people. Cell-based therapies, particularly those leveraging induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) transplantation, and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, have emerged as promising treatment modalities that may preserve, replace, or partially restore retinal function. However, these approaches face significant challenges in patient stratification, manufacturing consistency, surgical precision, and long-term outcome monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI), encompassing machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and computer vision, is increasingly being integrated across the cell therapy pipeline to address these limitations. This review comprehensively explores the role of AI in enhancing cell-based retinal therapies, spanning disease diagnosis and patient selection, stem cell quality control and differentiation optimization, CRISPR off-target detection, retinal organoid characterization, scalable manufacturing, and post-transplantation monitoring through multimodal retinal imaging. Throughout, we distinguish direct retinal cell-therapy evidence from retinal-adjacent, cross-domain, and conceptual evidence. We also propose an AI-powered end-to-end pipeline that connects patient profiling through gene editing, cell production, and transplantation to longitudinal outcomes tracking (a forward-looking framework that needs to be clinically validated in future). While AI offers powerful tools to enhance efficacy, reproducibility, and personalization, it does not replace the clinical and biological foundations of cell therapy. Critical challenges remain, including data scarcity, algorithmic interpretability, regulatory compliance, and clinical validation. This review concludes that the strategic integration of AI has plausible potential to become supportive infrastructure for scalable and reproducible cell-based treatments for retinal diseases, although its necessity has not been demonstrated and prospective clinical validation is still required, and biological insight and rigorous empirical verification remain fundamental.

The industrial revolution is gaining acceleration and reshaping globally with the power of Artificial Intelligence (AI). The applications of AI playing a significant role in managing different sections of industries, whether it is production section, maintenance section or research section. The allocation of raw materials and finished products is also being taken care with the help of new advanced technologies such as IoT, AI/ML, robotics and automation. This paper is mainly focused on the impact of these new technologies on the management and economies of Indian industries. Focus is made on various sectors such as IT, manufacturing, supply chain management. The study explored the effect of AI and modern technologies on the decision making, sustainability, workers dynamics, resource management, economies variations by considering theoretical frameworks and actual related data available. A keen observation on the issues and limitations of these modern technologies are also examined.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in organizations is transforming organizational roles, relationships, and balances of power and authority. This chapter examines how AI can be positioned not merely as a traditional technological tool, but as an organizational actor that participates in decision-making, knowledge production, coordination, and action processes. This transformation necessitates the redefinition of employees’ roles and the reconfiguration of collaborative relationships between humans and AI. The chapter first evaluates the opportunities offered by AI to organizations, along with its potential key risks. It then examines the evolving role of AI, from a tool to an assistant and subsequently to a team member/business partner, and discusses the organizational implications of human-AI collaboration. In particular, the increasing integration of AI into organizational processes is examined in terms of power, control, authority, responsibility, and accountability relationships. Finally, employees’ perceptions of AI are addressed, emphasizing the importance of organizational acceptance. In summary, this chapter examines the transformation of AI’s role in organizations and human-AI interaction, with a particular focus on the implications of this transformation for organizational processes, employees, and organizational structures.

With the continuous development of new technologies, these new technologies have a profound impact on the labor market. This paper uses micro-individual data from the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) from 2016 to 2022 and provincial-level macro-data on artificial intelligence (AI), employing a two-way fixed-effects model to systematically examine the actual impact and underlying mechanisms of AI development on the employment quality of workers. The study shows a significant positive correlation between the level of regional artificial intelligence development and the employment quality of local workers. However, this overall effect at the regional level cannot directly prove the individual-level effect of enterprises or employees using artificial intelligence. Mechanism testing further confirms that the effect of the regional AI development on improving the employment quality of workers is mainly achieved through optimizing the industrial structure and promoting the intelligentization of workers’ working mode. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that the regional artificial intelligence has a greater positive impact on employment quality for male workers, outside-system workers, and workers in the eastern region. Therefore, to achieve higher-quality employment for workers, it is necessary to promote the deep integration of AI with the real economy, build a multi-party collaborative education mechanism involving government, enterprises, and universities, and implement policies to promote digital inclusion and differentiated support.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI), digital transformation, and technology-driven economic systems has fundamentally reshaped global higher education dynamics, particularly within conventional economics and business programs. This study investigates the phenomenon of structural enrollment decline in economics and business higher education during the artificial intelligence era through a longitudinal institutional analysis of the Accounting and Management study programs at STIE Mulia Pratama, Indonesia, over the 1998–2025 period. Employing a quantitative longitudinal approach, the study utilizes institutional enrollment data obtained from the Indonesian Higher Education Database (PDDIKTI). Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, trend analysis, linear regression, forecasting analysis, and interpretative analysis to identify long-term enrollment transformation and institutional sustainability challenges. The findings reveal three major enrollment phases consisting of growth, fluctuation, and persistent structural decline. Regression analysis confirms statistically significant negative enrollment trends within both study programs. The Accounting program experienced an average annual decline of 3.356 students, while the Management program demonstrated a stronger annual decline of 5.056 students, indicating higher vulnerability to technological disruption and changing educational preferences. The study further reveals that AI disruption, employability orientation, digital economic transformation, and competency-based educational preferences substantially influence educational decision-making among younger generations. Consequently, conventional economics and business education increasingly faces sustainability challenges associated with declining institutional attractiveness and labor market transformation. This study contributes to the higher education literature by positioning declining enrollment as a manifestation of structural transformation rather than temporary institutional fluctuation. The integration of longitudinal institutional evidence, AI disruption perspectives, and sustainability analysis provides a broader analytical framework for understanding the future challenges of higher education within the digital economy era.

Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being developed for image acquisition, quantitative tissue assessment, diagnosis, and clinical prediction in rotator cuff tears. The breadth of this literature and its methodological limitations have not been integrated across the complete care pathway. Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library from inception to July 5, 2026 for English-language original studies applying AI to rotator cuff-related reconstruction, segmentation or quantitative imaging, diagnosis or classification, anatomical measurement, or prognosis. Two reviewers screened reports and extracted study, data, model, validation, reference standard, and performance characteristics. Diagnostic accuracy studies were assessed with QUADAS-2 and prediction-model studies with PROBAST. Because clinical tasks, modalities, models, reference standards, and reported metrics were not sufficiently comparable, evidence was synthesized narratively rather than pooled statistically. Results: Sixty-six reports were included: 35 diagnostic accuracy or classification studies, 20 segmentation or quantitative imaging studies, 9 prognosis or outcome prediction studies, 1 Magnetic Resonance Imaging reconstruction or image-optimization study, and 1 exploratory unsupervised-phenotyping study. Applications spanned Magnetic Resonance Imaging, radiography, ultrasound, computed tomography, clinical or multimodal data, motion video, and emerging sensing data. QUADAS-2 classified overall risk-of-bias as high in 27/36 diagnostic studies, unclear in 6/36, and low in 3/36. PROBAST classified all 8/8 completed prediction-model studies as high risk-of-bias; 1 protocol without model results was not rated. Promising internal performance was recurrent, but selection methods, imperfect or incompletely described reference standards, limited external validation, small or selected datasets, and analysis-stage weaknesses constrained clinical inference. Conclusion: AI has proof-of-concept value across rotator cuff imaging and decision support, but the current evidence does not establish routine clinical readiness or replacement of clinician judgment. Prospective multicenter studies, transparent reference standards, independent external validation, calibration and clinical-utility assessment, and standardized task-specific reporting are required.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Purpose: to identify, classify, and synthesize the application of artificial intelligence (AI) techniques in cryptography, including AI methods, cryptographic problems and applications, evaluation approaches, challenges, and emerging future research directions. Method: this study employed a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) following the PRISMA framework. Studies were retrieved from Scopus and analyzed through screening, quality assessment, data extraction, and thematic synthesis based on five research questions. Findings: neural networks, deep learning, and machine learning are the dominant AI techniques applied to cryptography, particularly in image encryption, privacy-preserving computation, healthcare, and IoT. Key challenges include computational overhead, methodological heterogeneity, reproducibility, and security validation, while emerging directions emphasize adaptive, privacy-preserving, and intelligent cryptographic systems. Implications: provides an integrated framework for understanding AI applications in cryptography and identifies key methodological patterns, challenges, and research opportunities to guide the development of secure, efficient, and adaptive cryptographic systems. Originality: lies in providing an integrated synthesis that systematically connects AI techniques, cryptographic applications, evaluation approaches, challenges, and emerging research directions within a unified framework.

Intermittent renewable generation, volatile loads, and concerns over grid stability have become defining features of modern power systems. Addressing these challenges with Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) is attracting growing attention, including through better forecasting, automated demand response, optimized energy storage, and smart grid fault detection. This paper highlights the various AI-based techniques developed across the smart grid landscape, ranging from solar and wind forecasting to short-term load forecasting, demand-side management, electricity price forecasting, energy storage and battery management, grid resilience, and digital twins. It offers an overview of recently published work, including the major approaches, namely deep learning (LSTM and Transformer models), explainable AI, multi-agent systems, reinforcement learning, and federated learning, together with their strengths and limitations. The paper also presents a conceptual three-layer framework comprising edge sensing, federated forecasting and control, and explainable operator support at the distribution-utility level; the framework is not validated empirically. Challenges such as data privacy, model interpretability, scalability, and cybersecurity are explored, together with future research directions and the relevance of these technologies to India’s energy transition goals.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming bioengineering, with applications ranging from diagnosis and biomedical imaging to wearable technologies, rehabilitation, biomaterials, biofabrication, and digital twins. This narrative review aims to examine the major innovations, challenges, and future directions of AI-enabled bioengineering, with particular attention to its clinical and translational development. The literature was searched in Scopus and PubMed, with emphasis on systematic reviews and meta-analyses and consideration of other relevant secondary literature across the main bioengineering domains. A total of 57 secondary publications were included in the principal evidence base. The review process was additionally informed by the ANDJ Narrative Review Checklist and an established qualification and scoring methodology applied to the selected secondary literature. The reviewed evidence shows a broad expansion of AI applications and increasing integration of intelligent technologies into bioengineering systems. However, important challenges remain, particularly regarding data quality and representativeness, validation and generalizability, reproducibility, safety, human oversight, ethical responsibility, equity, and regulatory requirements. Future developments are expected to increasingly involve multimodal, adaptive, connected, and human-centered systems integrating AI with sensing technologies, robotics, digital twins, and longitudinal data. Overall, AI-enabled bioengineering is progressing from promising technological applications toward increasingly integrated and translational systems. Its successful evolution will depend on combining technological innovation with robust clinical evidence, responsible development, and appropriate ethical and regulatory frameworks.

Technology and Human Factors in Education and Health

documents.abstract: Background. Transcriptomic data show which genes are active in cells and tissues. Machine-learning and deep-learning methods use these data to classify samples, integrate different datasets, and predict biological properties and treatment response. In oncology, a major challenge is transferring patterns identified in experimental models to tumor samples from patients. Objective. To critically synthesize current artificial-intelligence methods for transcriptomic analysis, with emphasis on oncology applications, transfer of models to patient data, and requirements for clinical validation. Materials and Methods. We performed a critical narrative review of primary studies and methodological papers and additionally described the authors' publication sample for 2021–2026. The literature review was updated through August 13, 2026. Results. The most developed areas include single-cell data analysis, spatially resolved tumor diagnostics, and drug-response prediction. Independent comparative evaluations show that increasing model size and complexity does not guarantee better performance than simpler methods. Clinical translation requires accounting for cellular composition and technical differences between measurement batches, aligning experimental and clinical response measures, preventing information leakage, and performing external validation. Conclusion. Artificial intelligence should be viewed as a data-analysis tool rather than a substitute for experimental or clinical validation. Its value depends on data quality, correct task definition, and the ability to maintain performance in independent cohorts.

Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The construction industry, which creates 13% of the world’s GDP, suffers from cost overruns of 28% and delays of over 42%, yet is still undigitized. AI has the promise of transforming management in the areas of cost, time and safety. This research provides a systematic review of AI applications and performs an original machine learning analysis on seven algorithms, i.e., Support Vector Machines, Logistic Regression, K-Nearest Neighbors, Random Forest, Stacking Ensemble, Artificial Neural Networks, and XGBoost on 139 Indian road projects with 44 risk factors. XGBoost performed the best with 82.50% accuracy and 84.21% F1-score. The most important concerns were the delay in decision-making (0.152), cash flow problems (0.082) and cost underestimate (0.071). Case studies demonstrate AI’s capabilities: 98.7% accurate cost estimation, 94.36% delay prediction via deep learning, and 97% safety monitoring with computer vision. These findings underscore the importance of ensemble ML in proactive, data-driven risk management, bringing projects into a predictive framework rather than reactive.

Developing a new medicine takes years of research and requires many decisions along the way. Researchers must identify a promising biological target, find or design a suitable compound, test its safety, and determine whether it benefits patients. Artificial intelligence (AI) is beginning to support each of these steps. Machine-learning systems can analyse large biological and chemical datasets, while newer generative models can suggest molecules for further study. AI can also help predict drug properties, identify possible new uses for existing medicines, and improve aspects of clinical-trial planning. These developments are encouraging, but they need to be viewed realistically. A computer-generated prediction is only a starting point: it must be tested in the laboratory and, ultimately, in people. AI systems can also be affected by incomplete or biased data, may not work well on unfamiliar problems, and can be difficult to interpret. This review discusses how AI is being used across drug discovery and development, what its current strengths and limitations are, and what will be needed for its responsible use. The central message is that AI is most valuable when it works alongside experimental science and clinical expertise—not as a replacement for them.
